summary: Interactive web platform for planning extravehicular activity (EVA) traverses and human survival on Mars. Designed as an aerospace HUD console, it combines multispectral 2D orbital cartography, biophysical life-support simulation, AI-generated voice briefings, and an immersive 360° Martian Street View powered by real NASA/JPL mosaics and live telemetry feeds.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
M.A.R.T.E. (Martian Analysis for Routes & Terrain Explorer) is a browser-based planning console for Mars surface exploration. It layers NASA/USGS orbital data on an interactive map (MOLA topography, THEMIS/HRSC imagery, geology, subsurface ice, weather and radiation) and lets a crew plan a route. It includes two hyperlocal Marswalks (Mount Sharp boxwork, 1.2 km; Kodiak delta, 0.9 km) and four rover traverses (14–31 km) across Jezero, Gale and Valles Marineris. For each route it computes distance, ETA, oxygen use, battery, effective load at 0.38 g, metabolic rate, radiation dose, nearest radiation shelter and a walk-back safety limit. The user can choose crew size (2–6), foot or rover mode, departure window and cargo, draw custom routes, simulate a solar particle event, and export or import the plan as JSON. A 360° viewer with six stations built from real NASA/JPL panoramas, plus a helmet-visor HUD, shows what the astronaut will see on arrival.

What benefits does it have?
It puts terrain, hazards, consumables and radiation in one view at the scale of a single EVA, which global tools like Mars Trek don’t target. It also works offline as a PWA, which matters when connectivity is limited.

What is the intended impact?
To help crews and mission planners reason about safety trade-offs (distance from shelter, slope, load, timing) before a Marswalk, and to inspire students and the public to explore Mars with real NASA data.

Tools, languages, hardware and software
Vanilla JavaScript (ES modules), HTML5 Canvas/SVG/<dialog>, CSS3, Leaflet 1.9.4, Vite 6, a Service Worker (PWA), USGS Astrogeology WMS, NASA Images API and NASA/JPL panoramic mosaics. No special hardware is required.

How is it creative?
It treats the map as a mission HUD rather than a viewer: a visor-style interface, a street-view-like 360° walkthrough of each station, and a simulation that lets you trigger a solar storm and see the nearest shelter and dose change in real time.

Factors the team considered

Astronaut safety first: radiation, shelters, slope limits, oxygen reserve and a walk-back limit, human factors: spacesuit mobility, carried mass and metabolic load, scale: from 1 km EVAs to 30 km rover traverses, transparency: we distinguish measured NASA data (basemaps, panoramas, the Curiosity RAD-based dose baseline) from mission-design scenarios (route geometry, hazard zones and shelter shielding values), which are illustrative.
